articles.title: Mudslide kills 1 and leaves 11 missing in China
articles.description: A mudslide in eastern China has killed one person and left 11 others missing. The disaster, which occurred Saturday in Suichuan County, Jiangxi province, followed days of heavy rain from tropical cyclone Saudel. Rescuers have moved residents to safer ground to prevent further danger. Two people were rescued alive. Typhoon Saudel previously made landfalls in Zhejiang province and later in Fujian province as a tropical storm. In Fujian, local authorities reported multiple residents missing and over 100 houses collapsed. A breached dike flooded villages. About 600,000 residents were evacuated. Streets have turned into rivers, and rescuers are using inflatable boats.

articles.title: Life uses 4 DNA letters. Scientists just made 8 work
articles.description: Researchers at UC San Diego have demonstrated that a key cellular enzyme can accurately read an eight-letter genetic alphabet, doubling the four letters used by all known life on Earth. The finding brings scientists closer to building expanded genetic systems that could perform entirely new biological functions.

articles.title: Horoscope for Saturday, September 05, 2026
articles.description:
Moon Alert

Avoid shopping (except food and gas) and important decisions from 3:30 a.m. to 10 a.m. After that, the moon moves from Gemini into Cancer.

Aries (March 21-April 19)

An average day

Today you're more sensitive about home and family and might feel hurt if someone makes a disparaging remark. Conversations might be confusing. Someone might make an assumption. Don't agree to anything important today. Just kick back and relax.

Taurus (April 20-May 20)

A positive day

Your imagination is activated today, which is great for those of you involved with artistic projects. Many of you might spend time daydreaming today or being lost in a fantasy world. In the real world, make an effort to clarify communications because it's a "fuzzy" day!

Gemini (May 21-June 20)

An average day

Conversations with friends, as well as groups and organizations, might be a tad confusing today. You might be dealing with someone’s idealism, or perhaps you are the idealist who confounds someone else. Keep things light because this is a playful, fun-loving day.

Cancer (June 21-July 22)

A positive day

Today the moon is in your sign at odds with fuzzy Neptune, which can induce a dreamy state of mind. It can also lead to bad decisions that require clear thinking. (It might distort your view of things.) Be careful with drugs and alcohol today.

Leo (July 23-Aug. 22)

An average day

Although your primary focus is on money, cash flow and your assets right now, today you might be caught up in mystical ideas or spiritual pursuits. If so, be aware that you are in a suggestible frame of mind. Things might not be as they appear. Tread carefully.

Virgo (Aug. 23-Sept. 22)

A positive day

You are strong and grounded today because both the sun and your ruler, Mercury, are in your sign. Nevertheless, the placement of the moon might create confusion in your discussions with friends and groups. You might assume something or be misunderstood. Double-check your communications.

Libra (Sept. 23-Oct. 22)

An average day

There is a curious astrological combination taking place today because in one way, you want to hide and be low-key. This is because of the placement of the sun. But in another way, you are high visibility, whether you like it or not. (In fact, some people know personal details about your private life.) This is because of the placement of the moon.

Scorpio (Oct. 23-Nov. 21)

A positive day

This is a feel-good day for you! If you can travel, that would be perfect because you want some adventure — something different. Go someplace you've never been before, even if it's in your own neighborhood. Do something curious or stimulating. Younger people will interest you.

Sagittarius (Nov. 22-Dec. 21)

An average day

This is a poor day to make important financial decisions about shared property, taxes, debt, mortgages, or anything jointly owned with someone else. Confusion, assumptions, misinterpretations, and even deceit are possible. Postpone important financial decisions for another day.

Capricorn (Dec. 22-Jan. 19)

An average day

Tread carefully today because the moon is opposite your sign, which is a tiny challenge. Generally speaking, it means you have to go more than halfway when you're dealing with others. You have to be accommodating. Furthermore, an element of confusion exists today. Be aware.

Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18)

An average day

You'd be smart to double-check your work today because confusion and misunderstandings can lead to problems. Assume nothing. Clarify all your instructions. Incidentally, this same advice applies to your health.

Pisces (Feb. 19-March 20)

A positive day

This is a tricky day for romance. You or your partner might over-idealize something. You might be disappointed because of unexpressed expectations. You might be disappointed because you had unrealistic expectations. Perhaps there's a plain old misunderstanding. Stay positive.

If today is your birthday

Actor Michael Keaton (1951) shares your birthday today. You're concerned with the happiness of others. You're empathetic, generous, and imaginative. This is a year of service, perhaps to family. Therefore, take care of yourself so you can support others when they turn to you for guidance, comfort, solace and courage.

articles.title: Have you been swarmed by biting flies? Why they're 'no joke'
articles.description:
From Rogers Park to Calumet, many people in the Chicago area are reporting a surge in flies.

Are there more flies, especially ones that bite?

The public health departments of Chicago and Illinois don’t track biting flies. But anecdotally, they seem ubiquitous. Social media is buzzing with people lamenting getting attacked by flies everywhere from Belmont Harbor to Logan Square.

“Today at a park in West Town I got swarmed by like seven flies after sitting on the ground for less than five minutes with my dog. Those bites are no joke,” wrote one Reddit user this week.

Another Reddit user had to leave Oak Street Beach, “because there were hundreds of flies that kept landing on me and staying on my skin. Felt like tiny needles. I’ve never experienced this at the beach.”

Lifeguards at lakefront beaches have been spotted wielding flyswatters and flies are swarming dogs on walks.

Why are there more flies?

Very wet and hot weather in recent months could be a factor.

This summer, the Chicago area has seen some of the most severe storms in recent years. It has also been very hot, with several heat waves.

Wet and warm conditions are typically good for breeding insects. But Nina Salem, founder of the Insect Asylum in Avondale, said favorable weather conditions vary for different species.

Yet Salem noted that she and other wildlife rehabilitators have been seeing a big uptick of “fly strikes.” That’s when flies lay eggs on animals such as squirrels and raccoons. After hatching, flies burrow into animals, alive and dead.

Salem cautioned against washing any affected animals because water will trigger hatching of eggs, which look like white rice.

What kind of flies are we likely seeing?

There are many kinds of biting flies, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health.

But the stable fly is a likely culprit because they peak in late summer and early fall. It’s gray with four dark stripes behind the head. This bloodsucker “will fly several miles to bite livestock (hence the name), pets and people,” said the department’s website. “They typically bite in early morning or late afternoon and often attack the ankles, inflicting a sharp, stabbing pain.”

Stable fly larvae “live in and eat decaying vegetation that washes up along the shore,” according to the National Park Service in Michigan’s Pictured Rocks. They don’t transmit disease to humans, but “are annoying enough to drive people away from beaches.”

Stable fly outbreaks have occurred along the shores of Lake Michigan, Chris Stone, medical entomologist at University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, wrote in an email. “This species is considered to be more abundant in years with high rainfall. So a peak this year would make some sense,” he said.

Other biting flies include deer flies, which are most abundant in the spring, as well as horse flies. Some horse flies are entirely black, while “greenheads” are light brown with shiny green eyes. Larvae live in water or moist locations.

Are fly bites especially painful?

They can be.

Stable flies suck blood through a pointed proboscis. “They have bayonet-like mouthparts with rasping teeth at the tip that they use to cut through or abrade the skin to create a pool of blood on which they feed,” Stone explained..

Deer and horse flies bite with “scissor-like mouthparts that cut into skin, causing blood flow which the flies lap up,” according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. This crude blood sucking can be especially painful.

What are officials doing about the flies?

Chicago Parks District “has not received an influx of concerns regarding the presence of biting flies, mosquitos and other insects in our parks,” Michele Lemons, director of communications, wrote in an email.

The parks department hasn’t seen park use drop. “In fact, for many of our programs, we saw an increase in participation this summer,” said Lemons.

But on Friday morning, Lake Forest Parks and Recreation department treated Forest Park Beach with an “EPA-approved product.”

The department said on Facebook, “While we can all agree our beach is amazing, the latest increase in fly activity is not!”

Indiana Dunes National Park warned about an outbreak of biting flies on Facebook, according to WBBM News Radio in Indiana. Park staff noticed a surge in biting flies on some eastern beaches about a week ago.

On Thursday, the Illinois Department of Public Health said it’s working on updating guidelines on managing flies and bites.

What can I do?

Most insect repellent doesn’t work on stable flies. Since they target legs and ankles, the National Park Service recommended wearing long pants and socks – not ideal for the beach.

In any case, stable flies can pierce through clothing, according to fly control company Spalding Labs.

Salem noted that parasitic wasps can eat flies. But if fly predators aren’t handy, she and Stone suggested treating clothes with permethrin, a chemical insecticide.

How long will this last?

A stable fly’s life span is 20 to 30 days. In the U.S, their peak season is July through September. But they can remain into October in warmer regions.

This summer, the Chicago area has endured heat waves, tornadoes, rainstorms, wildfire smoke and deafening cicada choruses. Now it’s biting flies. What’s next?

articles.title: 'No land left at all': Nepal flood survivors left with a transformed landscape
articles.description: Sheltering with relatives or in temporary camps, survivors of devastating floods in Nepal say they can no longer rebuild their homes after the landscape was violently transformed, leaving them focused simply on survival. Pabitra Lamsal had lived with her family in Dhunge Bazaar, in the Nuwakot district, for over 40 years. But the family’s two homes and her rice paddy fields have vanished, swept away by the floodwaters. People retrieve their belongings from a house in the aftermath of flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on September 3, 2026. —AFP/File “The river is flowing right where our houses used to stand,” the 45-year-old woman said, waiting at a government food distribution centre in Nuwakot. “There is no land left at all.” Along with the nine members of her family, she does not know where they will live. “You can’t think straight in a situation like this. We’ve rented two rooms for shelter, but we don’t have a stove to cook on, so we’re eating at a relative’s homes. The river swept away all the money we had.” People clear sludge from a house in the aftermath of flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on September 3, 2026. —AFP/File She leaves with a bag of rice, a packet of noodles, oil and biscuits. Nearby, gutted buildings, half-buried trucks, and mountains of mud bear witness to the violence of the floodwaters that swept everything away in their path. Army helicopters, deployed for rescue operations, fly overhead at regular intervals. The devastating August 26 flood, after a vast glacial mountain collapse high above on the China-Nepal border crashed into the river below, has killed more than 1,300 people and left more than 5,600 missing across both countries. The United Nations appealed Friday for $50 million to help more than 84,000 people in Nepal affected by the disaster. A general view shows damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of flash floods in Trishuli, Nepal’s Nuwakot district on September 4, 2026. —AFP Sumita Tamang, queueing for food supplies, said above all she wanted to find her missing husband, from whom she has heard nothing since the flood. “I’ve looked for him everywhere, but I still have no news of him. I hope he’s out there somewhere and will come home,” the 33-year-old said, her voice breaking through tears. “But I have absolutely no idea where he is. It’s been nine days.” ‘Lost everything’ For some victims, such as 47-year-old Rawendra Dawadi, headteacher of Trishuli Bazaar Secondary School, the flood was worse than a powerful 2015 earthquake which also devastated the region. “This disaster is far worse,” Dawadi said. “The school was completely destroyed by the earthquake, but we rebuilt it. Back then, we still had the land; this time, we’ve lost the land as well as the building.” Dawadi said he needed a new site before the school could be rebuilt. “This place is no longer safe,” he told AFP . People travel past damaged buildings following the deadly flash floods and mudslides in Nuwakot district, Nepal on September 3, 2026. —Reuters/File In the courtyard of Shree Chandrajyoti Secondary School, which is sheltering hundreds of displaced people from Nuwakot district, people queue for hot meals. One of them, 72-year-old Krishna Lal Chitrakar, said the land in Devighat where his home and those of his three sons once stood “has been turned into a riverbank”. “My father and four generations of my family lived in this spot,” said the man wearing a traditional Nepali topi hat. He is staying with 11 family members in a classroom where multiplication tables are posted on the walls. Families sleep on school benches with barely any belongings. He sits silently, while his wife, also in her 70s, wipes her eyes behind him. One of his daughters sobs uncontrollably. “We have lost everything,” he said. “But everyone is alive. Should I be happy or sad?” Header image: People stand next to damaged buildings following the deadly flash floods and a mudslide, in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal on September 4, 2026. —Reuters
